# The Agency You Hired Spent $50K. What Did You Actually Get?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-agency-spent-50k-and-i-have-nothing-to-point-at/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: A company can spend $50,000 on marketing, receive every promised campaign and report, and still be unable to say whether the work attracted a single valuable customer. That is not necessarily evidence that the agency is dishonest or ineffective. It usually means the money went out before anyone agreed what success would look like, who owned the accounts, or how results would be measured. Buyers are noticing: 39% of marketing leaders in Gartner's 2025 survey planned to cut agency budgets. Separate what the money bought, get the accounts and data back, agree what counts as a result, and only then decide whether to change agencies.

## Key points

- An agency can deliver everything it promised without helping the business grow; compare the work with the business goal, not the post count.
- Split the spend into agency fees, media and production, because each needs a different question.
- Media spend loses value before it reaches anyone: the ANA found only 36 cents of each programmatic dollar effectively reached consumers in its 2023 study.
- Impressions count displays, not people, and neither counts customers; agree the result that matters before the campaign starts.
- Every ad, analytics and creative account should be owned by the company, with the agency given access, not the other way round.

A company can spend $50,000 on marketing, receive every promised campaign and report, and still be unable to say whether the work attracted a single valuable customer.

That's not necessarily evidence that the agency is dishonest or ineffective. It may mean the company and the agency never agreed on what success would look like. We should separate the work completed from what actually changed for the business.

## First, what the $50K actually paid for

Imagine a small crypto exchange hiring an agency for three months. The agency launches advertisements, coordinates creator posts and delivers a monthly report. As an **illustrative example**, suppose $18,000 paid the agency, $24,000 was spent on advertising platforms and $8,000 paid for design and creator fees. These amounts are hypothetical, not a documented **lowob** client result.

| Line | Illustrative amount | What it bought | The question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agency fees | $18,000 | Strategy, management and reporting | Did the agency deliver the work it billed for? |
| Paid advertising | $24,000 | Ad placements on platforms | Did the advertising reach appropriate people? |
| Production | $8,000 | Design, videos and creator fees | Did the creative explain the product? |

Each expense deserves a different question. Most importantly, what was the work supposed to accomplish?

The media line deserves a closer look than most reports give it. When the ANA traced log-level programmatic data from 21 large advertisers in 2023, it found only 36 cents of each dollar spent through demand-side platforms effectively reached the consumer; the ANA points to supply-chain transaction costs and low-quality inventory, such as made-for-advertising sites, as the main leaks. A small company buying mostly on self-serve social platforms will lose less in the chain, but the lesson holds: "spent on ads" and "seen by the right people" are different numbers. Ask which campaigns actually ran, what was paused or rejected, and where the placements appeared.

## What counts as a result

A report showing 500,000 impressions tells you ads appeared on screens about that many times. It does not mean 500,000 distinct people saw them or that anyone became a customer. Platforms count reach, the number of unique people shown an ad, separately from impressions, which include repeat views by the same person. A report showing website visitors is a little more useful, but it still doesn't tell you what happened after they arrived.

For a DeFi lending protocol, a meaningful result might be someone making a first deposit and remaining active after a month. For a fintech app, it could be a verified customer making a transaction. For a business selling payments infrastructure, it might be a conversation with a company that has the budget and authority to buy.

That doesn't make awareness unimportant. If you hired an agency to help potential customers understand a new category, reasonable evidence may include relevant reach, message recall, or qualified inquiries. The key is to decide on the goal together *before* the campaign starts.

| Job the agency was hired for | Evidence that fits the job | Evidence that does not prove it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awareness in a new category | Relevant reach, recall, branded search, qualified inquiries | Raw impressions or total views |
| Creator or community programme | Quality and number of useful posts, creators worth keeping | Follower counts of the creators |
| Acquisition | Funded accounts, first transactions, active users after 30 days | Clicks and cost per click alone |
| B2B pipeline | Qualified conversations with buyers who have budget and authority | Form fills and downloads |

The evidence should match the job. Supplier case studies often report a falling cost per click without saying how many customers the clicks produced; a lower price for a visit is a real gain, but it is not the same as a customer. Our piece [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) sets out the measures that show something happened, and [what lead source attribution is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) covers how to record where customers came from, and where that record misleads.

> The most valuable thing in an agency's report isn't a large number. It's an explanation of what happened, what remains uncertain and what the company should change next.

## This week: get the accounts and the data back

Before any decision about the agency, make sure the company owns what the money built. Ad accounts, analytics, tag managers, pixels, creative files and reporting dashboards should sit in the company's name, with the agency given access. Meta's business tools are built this way: an owning business grants a partner agency access to specific tasks, such as advertising or analysis, and can remove the agency from the asset. An agency cannot pass on access to assets it only holds as an agency. If the agency owns the ad account, it owns the history.

The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey found data ownership was one of the reasons large advertisers bring work in-house: they want to own, control and protect their first-party data. A small company does not need an in-house agency to get the same protection. It needs the accounts opened in its own name and a contract that says so. The ANA's 2023 media buying contract template goes further, with audit rights, a schedule of transaction data to obtain from vendors, and a requirement for the advertiser's prior consent before an agency uses AI applications in delivering services. Our piece [Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) lists the accounts, records and routines to own.

Then instrument what matters: the one action that counts as a result, tracked in the company's own systems, from the source of the visit to the outcome. Without that, the next $50,000 will produce the same argument.

## Four questions to ask before changing agencies

**What did we agree to buy?** Compare the actual contract and campaign brief with the delivered work. Was it content, awareness, new users, or qualified sales inquiries?

**Where did the budget go?** Separate the agency's fees, media spend and outside costs. Ask which campaigns actually ran and what was paused or rejected.

**What can we measure?** Pick a meaningful action for the business. Show the direct evidence, and explain anything the data cannot establish.

**Can the current agency improve?** Clearer goals, better reporting or account access might solve the problem. A new agency won't fix an unclear assignment by itself.

Gartner's survey covered mostly larger companies, not early-stage startups, but the 39% planning cuts reflects an expectation that applies at every size: clients want to understand what they are getting for the money. Switching has costs of its own, in time, lost history and a new learning curve, so make the first three questions settle the fourth.

Paid advertising does not always have to come last. A fixed fee is not automatically better than every other contract model. The fair test is whether the arrangement is transparent, suitable for the work, and helps both sides make better spending decisions. Our guide to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) covers what each fee model rewards, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to set a budget against cost per qualified outcome.

The most valuable thing in an agency's report isn't a large number. It's an explanation of what happened, what remains uncertain and what the company should change next.

## lowob takeaways

- **An agency can deliver what it promised without helping the business grow.** Compare the work completed with the business goal, not just the number of posts or ads.
- **Know what the money bought.** Separate what the agency charged from the money spent on ads, production and creators.
- **Ask what people did after seeing the marketing.** A click is not automatically a funded account, an active wallet, or a qualified customer.
- **Keep access to your accounts and data.** An agency can run campaigns without controlling the only copy of your reports, accounts and creative files.

## Common questions

### What should I do if my marketing agency is not getting results?

First separate what the money bought: fees, media and production. Then get every account into the company's name, agree in writing what counts as a result, and instrument it. Only then decide whether the current agency can improve with a clearer brief.

### Who should own the ad accounts, the agency or the client?

The client. Ad, analytics and creative accounts should be opened in the company's name, with the agency granted access. Platforms such as Meta support this: the owning business grants and removes partner access.

### What is the difference between impressions and reach?

Impressions count how many times an ad was displayed, including repeat views. Reach counts unique people shown the ad. Neither tells you whether anyone became a customer.

### How do I measure whether an agency is worth the money?

Agree before the campaign which action counts as a result for the job the agency was hired to do, such as a first deposit, a qualified conversation or relevant reach for awareness, and track it in your own systems.
